strengths: Significance: Decisive error localization in multi-agent systems is an important operational problem, and compact reusable error schemata are an intuitive, potentially useful alternative to supplying entire historical trajectories.

Originality: The combination of LLM-generated failure schemata, semantic retrieval, and cache management offers a recognizable systems contribution, while the proposed synthetic benchmark could be valuable if reconstructed with leakage-resistant splits and stronger validation.

Empirical breadth: The evaluation covers WHO&WHEN, seven additional task datasets, multiple open and closed models, exact and tolerance-based localization metrics, and several cache/transfer ablations. Many reported improvements are substantial.
Presentation: The main motivation and online retrieval pipeline are generally easy to follow, and the appendix provides the principal schema-generation and diagnosis prompts.
weaknesses: Soundness—evaluation leakage: The paper only states that a trajectory cannot retrieve its own schema. It does not define train/validation/test splits or prevent retrieval of schemata derived from closely related test trajectories. More seriously, CORRECT-Error is created by matching successful trajectories to seed error patterns and injecting those patterns, after which CORRECT is evaluated by retrieving schemata from this same collection. Sibling examples derived from the same seed can therefore expose the generating error pattern, agent, and location. Since schema outputs explicitly contain the ground-truth agent and step number, this transductive setup can directly reward dataset-specific label regularities. The central accuracy and generalization claims are unsupported without splits grouped by seed schema, task/template, and generation lineage, plus evaluation on wholly unseen natural failures.

Soundness—task-definition inconsistency: A decisive error is formally defined as one whose correction changes a failed outcome to success, yet Figure 11 analyzes injected errors that do not affect the final outcome, and the benchmark construction does not report counterfactual replay verifying that each injected action is decisive. The known injection position is not automatically the earliest outcome-changing error, so benchmark labels may not represent the stated target.

Benchmark validation is inadequate: Asking annotators whether a trajectory is synthetic or genuine measures distinguishability, not whether the injected step is erroneous, earliest, causal, or correctly explained. No expert localization agreement against the synthetic labels is reported. The confusion-matrix values are also interpreted incorrectly as roughly 50% conditional performance even though they appear to be joint percentages, and the claimed 94.4% majority-fooling rate conflicts with Figure 12, whose 42.3% and 52.9% bars sum to 95.2%.

Several results and claims are internally inconsistent. The text says the retrieved-schema method reaches 71.5% and 104% of oracle performance in Figure 10, but the plotted per-dataset values do not show 71.5%. Calling a trajectory's own ground-truth schema an upper bound is questionable when the retrieved method can exceed it. Likewise, the paper alternates between one schema per cluster and generating a schema for every annotated trajectory, leaving the implemented method unclear.

The comparisons do not isolate the source of improvement. CORRECT uses GPT-5 to transform labeled examples while the fine-tuning and naive-ICL baselines are minimally specified, and there are no matched-token or matched-LLM controls such as summarized demonstrations, label-only nearest neighbors, random schemas, schemas with agent/step fields removed, or retrieval based only on pre-error context. Consequently, gains cannot confidently be attributed to transferable structural knowledge.

Reproducibility is insufficient: The manuscript provides no code or dataset access information and omits cluster algorithm and threshold, cache cardinalities, similarity preprocessing, retrieval details, schema filtering procedure, dynamic-management thresholds, candidate counts, decoding settings, per-dataset sample sizes, split construction, and fine-tuning configuration. Although five runs are claimed, no standard deviations, confidence intervals, or statistical tests are shown.

Efficiency claims are unevidenced and sometimes overstated. The system requires labeled trajectories, GPT-5 schema generation, embeddings, retrieval, and additional prompt tokens, yet no latency, token, monetary, memory, or amortization measurements support “subseconds,” “near-zero overhead,” “zero training costs,” or cheap scalability. The proposed online expansion and hot-schema distillation mechanisms are not experimentally evaluated.

Presentation and scope: The paper repeatedly claims broad generality and near-human performance, but reports no human localization baseline, little natural cross-application testing, and mostly synthetic results. Important distinctions between relative-percent and percentage-point improvements are blurred, and no dedicated limitations section discusses transductive dependence, synthetic-data bias, annotation ambiguity, or reliance on proprietary models.

Research ethics are not adequately treated. The 120-hour human study lacks participant count beyond three labelers, expertise criteria, consent, compensation, and review/approval information. The manuscript also does not discuss privacy risks from caching raw operational trajectories or schemata, propagation of sensitive data, misuse of failure logs, licensing of the proposed release, or the risks of treating synthetic injected failures as representative of deployed-system incidents.

strengths: Originality/significance: Condensing recurrent multi-agent failure patterns into reusable schemata is an intuitive and potentially useful direction, particularly for installations where failures recur but retraining is impractical.

Soundness: The manuscript evaluates several model families and task domains, reports exact and tolerance-based localization metrics, and includes cache-size, schema-count, transfer, and oracle analyses.

Presentation: The overall extraction-retrieval-diagnosis pipeline is understandable, and the schema-generation and diagnosis prompts are provided. The attempt to scale decisive-error evaluation beyond the small WHO&WHEN benchmark addresses a genuine empirical bottleneck.
weaknesses: Soundness: The main evaluation appears transductive and vulnerable to label leakage. The authors generate schemata from all annotated trajectories and merely prevent a target from retrieving its own schema. Thus, test-set labels—including agent, step, reason, and closely related examples—populate the cache used at test time. No train/validation/test partition by task, error seed, or cluster is specified. With synthetic examples produced from shared human-error seeds, leave-one-out retrieval can exploit near duplicates rather than demonstrate generalization to unseen failures.

The benchmark does not establish the claimed label validity. The paper's definition requires a decisive error to be the earliest step whose correction changes failure to success, but the injection pipeline does not report counterfactual re-execution verifying this condition. Figure 11 explicitly includes “non-flipped” injections that do not alter the outcome, which are not decisive errors under the paper's own definition.

The human study tests whether annotators can guess whether text is synthetic, not whether the injected step is erroneous, causally decisive, correctly localized, or representative of the natural error distribution. Indistinguishability therefore cannot support the strong claims that annotations are precise and failures faithful. The study also omits sample size, sampling procedure, labeler qualifications, agreement statistics appropriate to the task, uncertainty, and significance tests.

Experimental comparisons are incomplete and poorly controlled. Fine-tuning and naive ICL are evaluated only for Qwen-2.5-7B with essentially no training, retrieval, or hyperparameter details. There are no stronger retrieval, summarization, nearest-neighbor, structured-log, or schema-ablation baselines to isolate whether the benefit comes from labeled retrieved hints rather than the proposed schema representation.

Reported results contain serious inconsistencies. The oracle discussion says the oracle is superior while claiming CORRECT obtains 71.5% and 104% of oracle performance; these values do not follow from Figure 10, where CORRECT even exceeds the supposed oracle on HotpotQA. Several numerical descriptions of Table 2 mix datasets and tolerance levels. No confidence intervals or statistical tests accompany averages over five runs.

The methodology is underspecified and internally inconsistent. Algorithm 1 says trajectories are clustered but then generates a schema for every annotated trajectory. The clustering method, thresholds, cluster counts, representative selection, cache split, retrieval details, schema filtering, and distillation evaluation protocol are absent. Dynamic expansion and hot-schema distillation are presented as core components but are not convincingly evaluated.

Reproducibility is inadequate: per-dataset sample counts and splits, full baseline prompts, decoding parameters, model/API versions, randomization details, fine-tuning configuration, hardware, latency, token usage by component, and code/data release information are missing. Hyperparameters are selected on datasets later used for evaluation, including HotpotQA, without a separate validation set.

The “near-zero overhead,” “subseconds,” “zero training costs,” and practical-efficiency claims are unsupported by latency, cost, memory, or token measurements. The paper itself reports spending more than three billion proprietary-model tokens to construct the benchmark, which makes the broad low-cost claim especially questionable.

Presentation is below acceptance quality: several figures are too small to interpret, terminology alternates between schema/schemata/template, grammar is frequently rough, and claims such as errors being “finite,” scalable to millions, or approaching human-level recognition are not established by the presented evidence.

Limitations and ethics are not appropriately treated. There is no dedicated limitations discussion, and the paper gives no information about annotator consent or compensation, dataset licensing and release constraints, privacy in collected trajectories, proprietary-model dependence, or risks from deploying an unreliable diagnostic system. Overall, the idea has merit, but the leakage-prone protocol and unvalidated benchmark undermine the central empirical conclusions.

strengths: Significance: Decisive error localization in multi-agent systems is an important and practically relevant problem, and the paper motivates the difficulty of diagnosing long, cascading execution traces well.

Originality: Condensing prior failures into reusable error schemata is an intuitive and potentially useful alternative to raw-trajectory in-context learning and model fine-tuning. The combination of schema retrieval, expansion, and distillation is a coherent framework.

Soundness: The reported results span multiple model families, two existing WHO&WHEN subsets, and seven task domains. Table 1 shows several meaningful exact-step gains, including GPT-5 improving from 18.3% to 38.1% on the algorithm-generated subset.

Presentation: The high-level motivation and three-phase design are easy to follow. Tables 1–2 expose both exact and tolerant localization accuracy, and the appendix supplies the main schema-generation and diagnosis prompts.
The attempt to create a larger error-localization resource is valuable, and the blinded human study at least tests whether annotators can distinguish synthetic from purportedly natural trajectories.
weaknesses: Soundness: The experimental protocol appears transductive and vulnerable to serious leakage. Appendix A.1 says all error schemata are generated before evaluation and only prevents a trajectory from retrieving its own schema. A test trajectory may therefore retrieve a near-duplicate schema generated from another test example, including its ground-truth error agent, step, and reason. No train/validation/test split by task, source trajectory, or error family is described. This is especially concerning because the synthetic examples are explicitly produced by transferring a small set of seed errors and the paper emphasizes high similarity among failures.

Soundness: The human study does not validate the benchmark labels required by the central task. It tests whether synthetic trajectories look human-generated, but does not establish that the injected step is actually the earliest decisive error under the paper’s counterfactual definition, that correcting it flips task failure to success, or that no earlier error exists. Realism discrimination cannot justify the claims of precise, unambiguous ground truth and faithful natural-error distributions.

Soundness: Several reported claims conflict with the displayed evidence. The Figure 10 discussion states that CORRECT reaches 71.5% and 104% of oracle performance, but the plotted GAIA, HotpotQA, and WikiMQA values do not show 71.5%, and CORRECT even exceeds the supposed oracle on HotpotQA. The Figure 7 narrative also mismatches the plotted model-specific values. These inconsistencies undermine confidence in the analysis.

Soundness: Baseline coverage and tuning are inadequate. Fine-tuning and naive ICL are evaluated only with Qwen-2.5-7B in Table 1; Table 2 provides only an underspecified judge baseline; and the more directly related attribution method cited as Ge et al. (2025) is not compared. Fine-tuning hyperparameters, splits, and model-selection procedures are absent, so the conclusion that standard supervised learning fails is unsupported.

Soundness: Results lack sample counts per task, uncertainty estimates, or statistical tests despite sometimes small apparent subsets and five stochastic runs. Acc@3 and Acc@5 can also be generous for short trajectories, yet trajectory-length distributions and chance baselines are not provided. Exact-step accuracy remains low on natural data, reaching only 17.2% on the human-crafted subset, so claims about practical, accurate diagnosis are overstated.

Reproducibility: Essential details are missing, including dataset splits, cluster algorithm and number of clusters, similarity construction, retrieval thresholds, cache parameters, dynamic-management settings, error-injection prompts, decoding parameters, precise model snapshots, fine-tuning configuration, and per-dataset sizes. The manuscript contains no accessible code/data artifact, while relying on an unversioned proprietary GPT-5 service.

Significance/evaluation: The advertised online cache expansion and schema distillation mechanisms are not evaluated. Likewise, claims of subsecond adaptation, near-zero overhead, and computational efficiency are unsupported by latency, token, memory, API-cost, or throughput measurements; generating the benchmark alone reportedly consumed over three billion tokens.

Originality: At its evaluated core, CORRECT is retrieval-augmented prompting over LLM-generated summaries of labeled examples. The paper does not sufficiently distinguish this from established case-based reasoning, retrieval-augmented generation, or memory systems, and does not ablate schema content against matched-length summaries, error reasons, or other compressed exemplars.

Presentation: The manuscript is readable at a high level but contains frequent grammatical issues, imprecise terminology, and methodological contradictions—for example, Algorithm 1 first describes one representative schema per cluster but then generates a schema for every annotated trajectory. Figure 5 combines unrelated plots under one caption, and some small figure labels are difficult to read.

Ethics and limitations: There is no substantive limitations or ethics discussion. The paper omits human-study recruitment, expertise criteria, compensation, consent or review procedures; dataset licensing and privacy considerations; risks of exposing sensitive execution logs to proprietary APIs; and the environmental or financial implications of the stated three-billion-token generation process. No direct ethical violation is demonstrated, but the reporting is insufficient for evaluating the study responsibly.

strengths: The paper targets an important, practically relevant problem: localizing the earliest consequential error in long multi-agent trajectories could support debugging, recovery, and safer system updates.

The retrieval of compact error schemata is intuitive, lightweight, and potentially useful. Evaluations span several model families, seven task datasets, WHO&WHEN, and two additional benchmarks, with cache-size, truncation, retrieval-noise, and transfer analyses.

The manuscript is generally organized clearly and provides schema-generation, detection, and injection prompts, some fine-tuning hyperparameters, and an honest discussion of label ambiguity and multi-error failure cases.
The targeted-restart experiment is a promising attempt to measure operational utility rather than localization accuracy alone.
weaknesses: The evaluation appears transductive and highly vulnerable to leakage. The authors only exclude a trajectory's own schema; no independent train/test or seed-group split is described. Other cache entries can be near-duplicate failures, and synthetic examples derived from the same human error seed may occur on both sides of retrieval. Hyperparameters, including the number of retrieved schemata, are also selected using the evaluated datasets. Consequently, the results do not establish generalization to genuinely unseen failure structures.

The schemata themselves contain the labeled agent name and step number, as shown in the schema-generation prompt. In templated or structurally similar trajectories, retrieval can therefore transfer positional labels directly rather than provide abstract diagnostic knowledge. There is no ablation removing agent/step fields, no label-shuffled control, and no matched-length generic-guidance control. The oracle-schema result is particularly uninformative because an example's own schema explicitly contains its ground-truth step.

CORRECT-Error is not adequately validated as a benchmark of decisive errors. Its injection prompt modifies one message from an originally successful trajectory, but the paper does not show that downstream agents are re-executed or that correcting the injected action counterfactually flips the outcome, as required by the paper's formal definition. Asking annotators whether a trace looks synthetic tests stylistic detectability, not causal validity, annotation correctness, or agreement on the decisive step.

The human-study reporting is internally inconsistent: Section 4.2 says four labelers, then discusses agreement among five labelers, while Appendix Figure 8 ranges from zero to three labelers. The confusion-matrix percentages sum to 100 and are interpreted as though they were class-conditional rates; the assertion that performance is close to 50% 'in both cases' is not supported by the displayed 42.3/47.1/1.9/8.7 entries. These issues materially weaken the central high-fidelity claim.

Statistical support is insufficient. The paper reports medians over five runs but no dispersion, confidence intervals, or significance tests; dataset and split sizes are not given alongside most results. On the small WHO&WHEN human subset, several apparent gains correspond to only a handful of examples. CORRECT-Error results emphasize Acc@3 and Acc@5 without exact-step accuracy or a random-step baseline, so large tolerant gains are difficult to interpret relative to trajectory length.

Important method details are inconsistent or missing. The text says one schema is generated per cluster, whereas Algorithm 1 generates one per annotated trajectory. The clustering algorithm, epsilon and resulting cluster counts, decoding settings, exact model/API versions, parsing rules, streaming protocol, and full human-evaluation protocol are unspecified. The claimed public-code link is blank, and the dataset is only promised for future release, preventing present reproduction.

The 'near-zero overhead' and online-adaptation claims are under-supported. A single API-cost comparison and an asserted latency percentage omit absolute latency, workload size, retrieval/index costs, and schema generation/distillation costs. The streaming table is non-monotonic and lacks appropriate baselines, while dynamic cache expansion and refinement are not convincingly evaluated end to end.

Originality is moderate: condensing annotated failures into retrieved textual guidance is a sensible application of retrieval-augmented prompting, but the paper does not isolate what is gained by the proposed schema representation over label transfer, prompt structure, retrieved summaries, or human taxonomies.

The ethics discussion is cursory. It omits annotator consent/compensation, privacy considerations for caching and releasing execution logs or user feedback, and security risks such as cache poisoning or adversarial schemata. These concerns are especially relevant because the online method trusts feedback to update a shared diagnostic cache. Overall, the idea is promising, but the leakage risks and invalid benchmark validation leave the central empirical claims unsupported.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: localizing the earliest consequential error in long multi-agent trajectories could support debugging, restart, and monitoring workflows.

The compact, retrievable error-schema representation is intuitive and interpretable. It is a plausible way to reuse prior failure knowledge without fine-tuning or inserting entire trajectories into the context.

The empirical scope is broad in appearance, covering multiple model families, seven task datasets, WHO&WHEN, and two additional external benchmarks. The cache-size, retrieval-noise, truncation, and cross-domain experiments are useful directions.
The appendix includes schema-generation and error-injection prompts, fine-tuning hyperparameters, a failure case, and an honest discussion of label ambiguity and retrieval limitations.
weaknesses: The central evaluation on CORRECT-Error is circular and does not establish generalization. Synthetic errors are created by matching successful trajectories to human error schemata, while CORRECT is evaluated by retrieving schemata distilled from annotated errors. Excluding only the exact test trajectory does not prevent leakage through trajectories generated from the same seed, schema, or source trajectory. No group-disjoint splitting protocol is reported.

The human study validates only whether synthetic trajectories look human-generated, not whether the injected step is actually the earliest decisive error, whether correcting it flips failure to success, or whether its stated reason is correct. Perceptual indistinguishability is therefore insufficient evidence for benchmark-label validity. The manuscript nevertheless concludes that the labels are precise and that the benchmark faithfully represents natural failures.

Reporting of the human study is internally inconsistent: Section 4.2 states that there were four labelers, the same section later refers to five labelers, and Appendix Figure 8 appears to report at most three predictions. Sample sizes, sampling protocol, annotator qualifications, compensation, full instructions, uncertainty, and a standard agreement statistic are absent. These discrepancies materially undermine the claimed validation.

The method description is inconsistent and underspecified. Section 3 says that one schema is generated per cluster, Algorithm 1 generates one for every annotated trajectory, and Appendix A.3 says that all error schemata are generated. The clustering algorithm, selected K values, epsilon, train/cache/test construction, schema-distillation procedure, replay split, output parsing, and several runtime thresholds are not specified sufficiently to reproduce the work.

The comparison is not controlled for supervision or compute. CORRECT uses ground-truth annotated trajectories and GPT-5-generated schemata, while the principal baseline is a direct detector and the fine-tuning comparison is limited to Qwen-2.5-7B. Calling the method training-free or zero-cost obscures its substantial labeled-data and closed-model requirements. The claimed negligible overhead reports only a small online API-cost change and an unquantified latency percentage, while excluding schema construction and maintenance costs.

Results are presented as medians over five runs without individual results, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Several improvements on the real human-crafted subset remain very low in absolute terms—for example, GPT-5 exact-step accuracy rises only from 8.6% to 17.2%—which does not support broad claims of accurate or reliable diagnosis. Some model/dataset combinations also regress.

The formal target is not convincingly operationalized. A decisive error requires a counterfactual intervention that changes a failed outcome to success, but the paper does not execute or verify this intervention when assigning synthetic labels. Its discussion of non-flipped injected errors and multiple-error trajectories further exposes a mismatch between the formal definition and the evaluated labels.

Originality is moderate rather than strong: the core method is retrieval-augmented prompting using LLM summaries of labeled examples. The paper does not isolate whether gains come from genuinely reusable structural knowledge, generic error-analysis instructions, retrieval of label-correlated agent/step information, or near-duplicate synthetic patterns. The schema itself explicitly includes the ground-truth agent and step number, increasing shortcut concerns.

The paper is not presently reproducible: the displayed code URL is blank, the dataset is only promised for future release, and essential dataset counts, splits, seeds, API versions, cache contents, and full evaluation details are missing. Numerous terminology, typography, figure-label, and numerical inconsistencies also make the presentation difficult to audit.

The limitations section acknowledges ambiguity and retrieval limitations but omits the most consequential threats: synthetic benchmark circularity, seed-level leakage, weak causal validation of decisive-error labels, dependence on proprietary models, and risks from treating passive user feedback as ground truth. Human-subject and data-governance details are also inadequate. These soundness and reproducibility problems outweigh the promising idea and prevent acceptance in the current form.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: localizing the earliest consequential error in long, cascading multi-agent trajectories. Distilling prior failures into compact, retrievable schemata is intuitive and potentially useful.

The evaluation has broad coverage, spanning multiple open and closed models, WHO&WHEN, seven CORRECT-Error task families, AgentErrorBench, category prediction, streaming adaptation, retrieval noise, cache size, and targeted restarts.

Several reported gains are substantial. For example, CORRECT raises GPT-5 exact-step accuracy from 8.6% to 17.2% on WHO&WHEN human-crafted errors and from 18.3% to 38.1% on algorithm-generated errors.

The framework is interpretable, requires no parameter training, and reportedly adds little online cost. The prompts, ablations, and candid discussion of ambiguous labels, retrieval limitations, and multi-error cases are helpful.

The contribution has moderate originality: although its components resemble retrieval-augmented case-based reasoning, applying distilled failure schemata to step-level multi-agent debugging is a promising direction.
weaknesses: The central evaluation appears transductive rather than cleanly held out. The cache is constructed from annotated trajectories, and the paper only excludes retrieval of the target's own schema. Near-duplicates or errors produced from the same human seed may therefore remain available, especially in CORRECT-Error. Seed-, cluster-, or temporal-level splits are needed to establish generalization to unseen failures.

Baseline resource parity is unclear. CORRECT receives labeled steps, error reasons, and GPT-5-generated schemata from the evaluation distribution, while competing methods may not receive an equivalent labeled-example or inference-compute budget. Describing the method as training-free understates this supervision and offline expense.

The synthetic-data validation measures surface authenticity, not label validity. Raters distinguish synthetic from human traces, but apparently do not verify that the injected step is erroneous, is the earliest decisive error, or counterfactually changes the outcome. It is also unclear whether downstream agents are rerun after injection; without replay, the claimed propagation may be artificial.

The human study is internally inconsistent: the main text mentions four labelers but later refers to five, while Appendix Figure 8 appears to cover only three. The confusion matrix also suggests a strong bias toward predicting “human”; near-chance aggregate accuracy under that bias does not establish indistinguishability. Sample counts, instructions, recruitment, compensation, agreement measures, and uncertainty are missing.

Some claims exceed the evidence. Exact-step accuracy remains only 12.1–17.2% on the human-crafted subset; “subsecond” adaptation is not measured; latency lacks absolute values; and the restart result reports a 10% to 20% change without sample size or uncertainty. Five-run medians are given without dispersion, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

The method specification has contradictions and omissions. Section 3.1 proposes one representative schema per cluster, whereas Algorithm 1 generates one per trajectory. The clustering setup, stopping threshold, filtering procedure, cache splits, failure handling, and total offline cost are insufficiently documented.

Reproducibility is currently inadequate: the abstract's code link is blank, the dataset is only promised for future release, exact GPT-5 versions are unspecified, and per-dataset sample sizes are absent. Several presentation issues further undermine confidence, including calling absolute percentage-point changes “relative improvements” and unexplained repeated values in Table 2.

The ethics discussion omits risks central to the proposed deployment: privacy and memorization when caching production traces, cache poisoning through erroneous or adversarial feedback, and consent or compensation details for expert annotators.
